paper_title: AgentRoom: Concurrent Multi-Agent Coding in a CRDT-Backed Shared Workspace

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Concurrent multi-agent coding promises division of labor across modules, robustness through redundancy, and parallel exploration at the natural granularity of multi-file projects. Realtime collaborative editing protocols solve this coordination problem for human teams via Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), but the LLMs underneath generate one token at a time and existing multi-agent coding systems inherit this serial limit: they either sequence agents through phase handoffs or pool independent samples without coordination, and a single agent abandons up to half of hard tasks with a one-file stub-and-exit. AgentRoom is a realtime collaborative editing protocol for concurrent coding agents. Its runtime layer exposes file-level claim, status, and broadcast as MCP tools on a CRDT-merged shared filesystem. Five frontier coding-CLI models ran four backend coding tasks, with cross-language checks in Python DevBench and Rust+axum. For CLI-stable models, AgentRoom with 2 agents abandons fewer tasks than Solo and has less run-to-run variation. At matched-compute, one positive mean LLM-judge contrast puts AgentRoom over parallel-merge. The other contrast, a bundle probe, puts full AgentRoom above each partial case: an ordering rather than a percentage split. Coordination, not parallelism or CRDT-merge, bears the load.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Multi-agent coding systems [Qian et al., 2024, Hong et al., 2024, Nguyen et al., 2024, Huang et al., 2024, Ishibashi and Nishimura, 2024, Pan et al., 2026, Islam et al., 2025, Peng et al., 2026, Zhu et al., 2025, Wu et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2025, Park et al., 2023, Chen et al., 2023, Shinn et al., 2023, Ashrafi et al., 2025, Grötschla et al., 2025, Shafin et al., 2025] predominantly use sequential turn-taking: design implement review, each agent waiting for the previous. Implicit concurrent coordination via CRDTs has been explored [Pugachev, 2025] but with mixed results (21% speedup / 39% slowdown across tasks). Whether explicit coordination on CRDT-merged shared workspace can outperform both the sequential and the implicit-CRDT alternatives at matched compute is the question we address. System. AgentRoom is state-management room for concurrent coding agents: structured runtime object with file-level claim semantics, an append-only broadcast log, and each agents status, exposed to agents as small set of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (room_claim, room_release, room_state, room_broadcast, room_read) on top of CRDT-merged shared filesystem [Shapiro et al., 2011, Jahns, 2024, Automerge Project, 2023]. Comparison. AgentRoom uses different coordination paradigm from CodeCRDT [Pugachev, 2025], which infers coordination implicitly and pre-assigns outliner and implementer roles: it replaces both with an explicit room and an advisory protocol (Section 2.3), without role pre-assignment or orchestrated handoffs. We make this comparison at matched compute in Section 4: the agents stay the same, but we combine them in different ways. Correspondence: sungle3737@gmail.com Preprint. Finding. We find that two agents in an AgentRoom suppress the lone-agent stub-andexit failure mode (the agent emits onefile source skeleton and exits early, judging the task too hard): across all 12 modeltask strata, the pooled Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) estimate puts Solos odds of abandonment at 13.7 times AgentRooms (95% CI [3.9, 48], < 105, Tarone homogeneity p=0.92). Solos abandonment odds exceed AgentRooms in every stratum with events (odds ratio above 1). Contrasts. Figure 6 in Section 4.1 breaks the results down by model and task. At matched compute, AgentRoom has +0.213 mean-quality advantage over parallel-merge on the continuous LLMjudge composite (Welch p=0.003, both Sonnet, structurally bias-immune; Figure 1). substrate-only bundle probe (Appendix B.13) supports the mean ordering shared-only < prompt-only < AgentRoom, with the larger observed step at the MCP coordination layer; at n=7 the interval on that step spans zero, so we read the split qualitatively. Figure 1: T4 six-condition coordination ablation: AgentRoom is the top condition, while concurrency without coordination (parallel-merge) and sequential hand-off (ChatDev-style) fall below the single-agent baseline.

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: 2.1 AgentRoom: CRDT-backed shared workspace AgentRoom is single integrated primitive (Figure 2): CRDT-mediated shared filesystem with concurrent agents plus coordination interface. We co-designed the three components below, and we do not ablate them separately. Shared Workspace + CRDT. All agents execute in W, and any file one agent writes is immediately visible to the others. pycrdt (the Yrs port [Jahns, 2024] of Y.js) merges concurrent writes within crdt=2 at the character level, and we add brace/paren-balance sanity check (Figure 3). through MCP server Coordination Interface. Agents access tools: room state room_claim(path) atomically assigns file ownership and rejects if another agent already holds the path; room_broadcast/read maintain an append-only JSONL message log; room_state exposes peer state; the interface enforces ownership at the state-management layer rather than relying on agent intelligence to parse text claims; this is the key distinction from chat-only multi-agent coordination (4.6). Figure 2: AgentRoom architecture: coding agents share workspace mediated by CRDT; the MCP server exposes claim, release, broadcast, state, read. 2.2 Formal model: collision rate and coordination layer Objects. Let = {a1, . . . , aN } be the agents, the file set, and Wt the workspace state at time t. What SEC does and does not buy. What does the substrate guarantee? An op-based sequence CRDT [Shapiro et al., 2011, Roh et al., 2011, Kleppmann and Beresford, 2017] underlies the substrate, stamping edits with Lamport timestamps [Lamport, 1978] and satisfying strong eventual consistency (SEC); SEC eliminates data loss under concurrent edits but is property over byte-level merge, not semantic compatibility: two agents inserting incompatible function signatures at the same character offset both survive in the merged file and break compilation downstream. Where the algebra lives. Appendix A.1 carries the full edit-set algebra and the SEC formalisation. 2 Figure 3: Real-time CRDT merge during single T4 Sonnet AgentRoom 2 run. The MCP-mediated chat (left) drives concurrent character-level edits in the shared file (right); both αs and βs insertions co-exist on the same line via the Yrs CRDT, with no byte-level conflict raised in this run. Per-message Bezier leaders link each chat broadcast to the code line it talks about. Coordination layer. Let Ct be the active claims and Lt the append-only message log. The room exposes three MCP tools: claim(f ) atomically maps AF{OK, CONFLICT}, broadcast(m) appends to Lt, and state() returns (Ct, L[tτ,t]) where τ is recent-log time window. Mutual exclusion. How strong is the lock? claim is atomic and provides mutual ex- (cid:12){i : (f, i) Ct}(cid:12) (cid:12) clusion under cooperationf, : (cid:12) 1. Following Chubby-style advisory locking [Burrows, 2006], we enforce at the prompt layer rather than in the kernel; SEC still preserves the bytes of an agent that writes without claiming, and the room log surfaces the violation for the cross-agent bug-fix pattern (Appendix C). Why is the substrate alone insufficient? Collision rate. Even under pairwise-independent per-agent policies (a lower bound; shared task/workspace bias makes the true rate higher), the probability that any two of agents target the same file from candidate pool of size Kt is pcollision(N, Kt) = 1 1 (cid:89) (cid:16) k=0 1 Kt (cid:17) , (1) which comes to 0.20 at our =2, Kt5 operating point. What collision costs. SEC merges colliding edits at the byte level but not at the intent level, so collisions typically break compilation or tests; the claim primitive drives this rate to zero at O(1) per-edit cost. Information density (motivational). Why should coordination help at all? Appendix A.2 gives an information-theoretic motivation for why coordinated concurrent edits should beat sequential edits at fixed compute: treating patches as random variables over the rubric-coverage space, the per-step joint information across agents scales near-linearly in when claims keep the joint entropy from collapsing. We present this as motivation for the bundle component probe rather than formal proof. It is per-step motivation only, not claim that end-task quality scales in ; the demonstrated operating point is =2, and quality declines beyond it (4.5). 2.3 Collaboration Protocol Workflow. Agents receive an advisory six-step workflow: (1) read room state before writing; (2) claim each file they plan to create; (3) on claim conflict, revise and pick different file; (4) write the claimed files; (5) poll for updates between subtasks; (6) report completion by broadcast. Rules in practice. The protocol has two standing rules. The room rejects claims for files already held by another agent. The prompt tells agents to read existing files before writing and to import from teammates code. The protocol is advisory at the prompt layer; agents typically deviate when teammate stalls, an informative pattern documented in Appendix C. Despite this imperfect adherence, we find that AgentRoom outperforms the no-coordination condition. 3 2.4 Baselines We compare AgentRoom against three alternatives at matched compute: Solo (single agent), Sharedonly (N agents on one shared CRDT workspace, no collaboration prompt, no MCP tools), and Parallel-merge (N agents in separate workspaces, post-hoc file union, later-timestamp tie-break). 2.5 Quality Score and Emergence Score Scorers. Every run produces quality composite in [0, 1]. We use three scorers with overlapping but distinct definitions; Appendix lists the full weights and dimensions. An LLM-judge scores the T4 budget-fair body cells (Sonnet 4.6 with fixed rubric over four dimensionsspec coverage, correctness signals, code quality, test rigorweights 0.35/0.30/0.20/0.15). For cross-validation we also compute regex scorer (five dimensions including test-pass-rate term) and an AST scorer (four dimensions over the TypeScript compiler API). The cross-model headline ES  (Table 2)  uses the AST scorer because ceremonial defensive code can game lexical pattern-matching; the matched-compute ablation  (Table 1)  is the LLM-judge composite, and the regex/AST composites in Appendix preserve the same condition ordering. Cross-validation. How well do the three scorers agree? LLM-judge correlates with the regex scorer at Pearson r=0.67 over the T4 runs both scorers see (n=246, App. E); regex and AST correlate at Pearson r=0.79, Spearman ρ=0.62 on 30-run cross-check. deterministic 1-file abandonment classifier decides the Tier CMH binary outcome (4.1), independently of these continuous quality scorers. The main directional findings (CMH OR= 13.7, AgentRoom > parallel-merge, AgentRoom > ChatDev) hold under the regex and AST scorers (Appendix E). Emergence score. The Emergence Score divides -agent mean quality by solo mean quality at the same model and task, ES = sN /s1, where ES>1 indicates multi-agent improvement. We report 95% bootstrap CIs on ES (10 000 resamples) for headline cells. Unless stated, =2. Judge sensitivity. Does the judge matter? To address same-family preference bias [Li et al., 2026, Wataoka et al., 2025] in the primary Sonnet judge, we re-scored 30-run T4 subset with two cross-judges: Claude-Haiku (Anthropic cross-model) and Codex GPT-5.4 (cross-vendor). Sonnet tracks Haiku at r=0.87 (n=30), Sonnet tracks Codex at r=0.86 (n=26), and Haiku tracks Codex at r=0.78 (n=26); the cross-vendor Codex judge is uniformly stricter, mean composite 0.151 vs Sonnet, but preserves the per-run ranking, so the composites ranking is stable across judge vendors. quota block kept Gemini-3-Pro out of the panel at experiment time. What does quality not cover? Throughout the paper, quality means this composite; its four dimensions do not measure maintainability, security, or long-term evolution cost, and the composite should not be read as software quality at large. 2.6 Tasks Task suite. What do the agents actually build? For the main task suite we use four Express.js/TypeScript tasks that span difficulty axis and distinct domain types; Appendix gives the T1/T2/T4 specs. T1 asks for JWT authentication across 6 files. T2 opens up marketplace API and wants 10 files. T4 demands double-entry financial ledger with multi-currency, hash-chained audit [Haber and Stornetta, 1991], reconciliation, and fraud detection, over 15 files. T5 pushes further, to an algorithmic trading platform with order matching, portfolio P&L, risk, market data, and accounts, again 15 files. Scope and budgets. We use fifth task T3 (collaborative e-commerce modules) only in the difficulty-gradient appendix (Appendix B), and we exclude it from the CMH pool. The four tasks span different application domains at progressively larger scope, and they share an Express.js/TypeScript runtime and the same sandbox template, but not the application logic. T1, T2 and T3 get 300 of wall clock, T4 gets 600 s, and T5 gets 900 s. Evaluation. The agents author their own vitest suites on top of the templates single smoke test, so we report raw pass counts descriptively only. We assess correctness and quality with the LLM-judge composite, then cross-validate it against the regex and AST scorers (2.5). We report small Python cross-domain check using DevBench [Li et al., 2024] (now DevEval) in Appendix B. Broader cross-language evaluation remains limitation (5). We draw the protocol as one runs swim lane in Appendix (Figure 9).

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: Which models? Five frontier coding models, three providersAnthropics Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5, OpenAIs GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4-mini, and Googles Gemini 3 Flash. The headline cells use the four CLI-stable models, and we exclude GPT-5.4-mini for vendor-CLI crash under concurrent MCP execution (4.4)a deployment caveat rather than an AgentRoom property. Access and pinning. Accessed via vendor CLIs in non-interactive mode with vendor-default sampling, versions pinned (Claude Code 2.1.119, Codex CLI 0.120.0, Gemini CLI 0.40.1; the per-run logs record model identifiers and per-agent invocation strings). No seeds are set: the models are proprietary and hosted, so we do not claim bit-for-bit reproducibility; we report run-to-run spread as σ throughout. Which conditions? AgentRoom: agents launched within 1 s, sharing and the room MCP server. Shared-only: same launch, no collab prompt, no MCP. Parallel-merge: solo agents in separate workspaces, post-hoc file union with later-timestamp tie-break. Wall-clock budgets: 300 (T1/T2/T3), 600 (T4), 900 (T5). Valid-run filter. We pool all attempts 30 elapsed; this excludes only the authentication and network failures that exit within the first 30 s. We do not apply additional file-count or test-count filters because earlier drafts found these biased against compact Codex/Gemini implementations. Headline cells use bootstrap 95% CIs (10 000 resamples) and σ where 3. We compute the Tier II LLM-judge cells on the budget-fair pool, and few runs completed after the pool was frozen preserve the direction but are not folded into the reported cells. Each table lists its own per-cell n; underpowered cells appear only in the appendix, flagged as exploratory. What do we measure? Continuous quality score [0, 1] produced by the LLM-judge of 2.5 applied to the post-run repository snapshot; emergence score ES(m, N, τ ) = sm,N,τ /sm,1,τ ; raw passing-test count from vitest; room-message count (broadcast and direct-send entries); CRDTconflict count (guard firings within crdt=2 s). Evidence tiers. We sort the results into three evidence tiersTier I, the judge-free binary abandonment outcome; Tier II, the continuous LLM-judge quality cells; Tier III, exploratory cross-model comparisons under the regex/AST scorer family. Primary scorer. The LLM-judge is the primary scorer for all T4 budget-fair statistics in Sections 44.3 and is cross-validated against the regex and AST scorers (2.5); cells outside the T4 LLM-scored pool (cross-model effect-size, difficulty gradient) are reported under the regex/AST scorer family in Appendix as Tier III exploratory.

sections.title: 4 Results
sections.content: We report the results in two tiers of decreasing statistical strength. Tier is the variance and abandonment-rate reduction, which replicates across all three CLI-stable models with scorerinvariant binary outcome. Tier II is the controlled six-condition ablation and the ChatDev paradigm contrast under our LLM-judge rubric (matched compute on the T4 fintech-ledger task). The crossmodel ES under the regex/AST scorer family and the cost-equivalent paired-model comparison are exploratory and reported in Appendix B. 4.1 Tier I: Variance and Abandonment-Rate Reduction at 2 What does second agent buy? Two agents in an AgentRoom cut run-to-run standard deviation by 3045% among in-budget non-failing runs (Figure 4) and eliminate specific lone-agent failure mode, 1-file abandonmenta sub-0.3 run that exits within 200 or leaves at most two source files, typically single stub emitted in the first 80 s. The result replicates across all three powered CLI-stable models (Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, Codex GPT-5.4) and both Tier tasks (T4, T5). On T4 Sonnet, solo σ=0.23 vs 2 σ=0.14. On T5 Sonnet, 0.23 vs 0.13. On T4 Haiku, the lone agent commits the 1-file abandonment on 12 of 35 attempts (34%) while AgentRoom 2 commits it 1 of 17 times (6%; Fishers exact one-sided p=0.025). The mean quality lift from 2 is noisier signal, so we report it as exploratory in Appendix B; the variance and abandonment results stand on their own. The variance-reduction direction is consistent with self-consistency [Wang et al., 2023] and mixture-of-agents ensembling [Wang et al., 2024], but AgentRoom achieves it through coordinated concurrent generation in shared workspace rather than independent sampling and aggregation. 5 Figure 4: Solo (slate) vs AgentRoom 2 (rust) score distributions for the three CLI-stable models on T4 (LLM-judge composite, budget-fair pool). σ contracts by 3045% under AgentRoom in every panel (Sonnet 0.230.14, Haiku 0.250.17, Codex 0.270.15); mean shift varies by model. Per-model and per-task abandonment. How is an abandonment labelled? deterministic codebook applied to per-run snapshot and CLI exit metadata labels each < 0.3 event as either 1-file abandonment or infrastructure failure; the codebook ships with the release, and Appendix B.12 sweeps its threshold sensitivity. The counts below compare Solo against AgentRoom 2 on the budget-fair pool under Fishers exact one-sided test; this pool covers every budget-fair run including those without an LLM score, so denominators differ slightly from Table 1. On T4 the reduction is individually significant for two models: Haiku falls from 12/35 to 1/17 (p=0.025) and Codex from 9/17 to 2/21 (p=0.005). The remaining two are directionally consistentSonnet drops from 6/33 to 0/17 (p=0.070) and post-MCP-fix Gemini (4.4) from 2/5 to 0/5 (p=0.22). Across tasks. On T5 all three per-model strata are directionally consistent but individually underpowered (per-stratum counts in Figure 6). Across all seven per-model strata every Solo abandonment count is the AgentRoom count; two of four are individually significant on T4. Pooled across strata. Stratifying by both model and task across all four Express.js task difficulties (T1/T2/T4/T5) gives 12 modeltask strata over the three powered models; with the deterministic classifier applied to all budget-fair runs, the Cochran-MantelHaenszel test yields common odds ratio of 13.7 (95% CI [3.9, 48]), χ2=22.8, < 105, with Tarone homogeneity p=0.92. The per-stratum effects are statistically indistinguishable. Robustness of the pool. The pooled effect is not carried by the small strata: T4-only CMH (3 strata) is OR= 11.9 [3.0, 47], p=5 105. Pooled per task, abandonment falls in every taskT4 32%5% (p=0.0001) and T5 23%0% (p=0.031) individually significant, T1 and T2 directionally consistent at small (Figure 6). The flat Fishers exact pooled count across all 12 strata (40/131 Solo = 31% vs 5/94 AgentRoom = 5%, p<106) is shown for completeness. Conditional quality. What happens once the catastrophic runs are set aside? On T4 Sonnet under the LLM-judge rubric, Solo averages 0.544 (n=32) where AgentRoom averages 0.669 (n=14), excluding catastrophic infrastructure-failure runs, so AgentRoom leads by +0.125; Welch t=2.30, p=0.022. AgentRooms catastrophic-failure rate on Sonnet T4 matches Solos because both encounter identical infrastructure failure rates; the abandonment failure mode (1-file stub-and-exit) is what AgentRoom actually defuses. 4.2 Tier II.a: Six-Condition Ablation Matched-compute ordering. Table 1 (T4, Sonnet 4.6, 600 budget, budget-fair pool 30700 s) compares AgentRoom against five alternatives at matched compute under the LLM-judge rubric. The six conditions form clean monotonic orderingChatDev-style sequential pipeline 0.333 (n=6) parallel-merge 0.456 (n=12) < solo 0.544 (n=32) < shared-only 0.575 (n=11) < shared+collab without MCP 0.588 (n=7) < AgentRoom 0.669 (n=14, σ=0.140). Parallel-merge contrast. Which contrast carries the most? The most informative single contrast is parallel-merge (concurrent without coordination) vs AgentRoom (concurrent with CRDT+MCP coordination); both run two Sonnet agents in parallel for the same wall-clock budget, but only AgentRoom has the shared CRDT workspace and explicit MCP signalling. AgentRoom leads parallel-merge by +0.213 in mean quality, Welchs t=3.35, p=0.003. Naive concurrent ensembling actually underperforms single agent 6 (0.456 vs solo 0.544) because without coordination the second agents server.ts silently overwrites the first agents file; PM amplifies rather than averages the stub-and-exit behavior. The shared-only condition sits between solo and AgentRoom (0.575), recovering some of the loss but not reaching the full bundle. Does it hold on other models? Appendix B, Table 8, reports the cross-model ablation on Haiku and Codex: Haiku replicates the pattern with AgentRoom 0.662 (n=17) above solo 0.530 (n=35); Codex posts the lowest solo mean of the four models at 0.384, consistent with its monolithic-architecture priors degrading multi-agent decomposition. Table 1: T4 Sonnet 4.6 six-condition ablation (LLM-judge composite, budget-fair 30700 pool). Parallel-merge vs AgentRoom: +0.213, Welch t=3.35, p=0.003. The shared+collab-noMCP probe ran under 1200 wall budget; its runs are filtered to the same 30700 envelope as every other cell (Appendix B.13). Cross-model replication in Appendix B, Table 8. Note

Why rebuild it instead of running the published one? To compare against the dominant prior paradigm of sequential role-based pipelines [Qian et al., 2024, Hong et al., 2024, Nguyen et al., 2024], we ran ChatDev-pattern baseline using the same model and CLI as AgentRoom (Sonnet 4.6 via Claude Code) instead of importing the published 2023 ChatDev framework, whose OpenAI-only client and unmaintained dependency stack would have introduced model-confound and version-rot. The baseline implements ChatDevs three-phase workflow faithfully (requirements analysis technical design implementation, with role-specific prompts and intermediate artifacts handed across phases) under 1200 budget that matches AgentRoom 2 compute. Of the 13 budget-fair ChatDev runs, 7 are infrastructure failuresevery phase agent exits with code 1 and zero output at 32 because the orchestrator crashed before producing code, and and we exclude them from the quality comparison, consistent with the infrastructure-failure exclusion in the Tier codebook, and no run in any other condition meets this criterion. Across the remaining n=6 genuine ChatDev runs (Sonnet, T4, budget-fair) ChatDev averages s=0.333 (σ=0.197) where concurrent AgentRoom 2 on the same task at the same compute reaches 0.669 (n=14, σ=0.140). Welchs t=3.78, two-sided p=0.006. Sequential pipelines amplify the lone-agent abandonment failure mode at every phase boundary: in the 6-run genuine subsample, 4/6 ChatDev runs produced 1-file implementation-phase abandonment that nevertheless passes the boilerplate GET / test, while AgentRoom 2 exhibited 0/10 such abandonments in the hand-inspected subsample. How should this be read? We read the ChatDev contrast as further evidence that AgentRooms coordination layer collapses this specific mode independently of upstream task structure, not that ChatDev pipelines have higher catastrophic-failure rates overall. 4.4 Tier II.c: Concurrent-MCP CLI Compatibility (deployment caveat) Gemini. Left: mean LLM-judge composite with σ band peaks at =2 then declines. Middle: mean tests passing peaks at =3. Right: AgentRoom message count rises super-linearly past =3, consistent with single-broadcast-channel coordination overhead. 4.5 Scaling and Heterogeneity How many agents is best? Sonnet T4 quality peaks at 2 then declines under the LLM-judge rubric0.544 / 0.669 / 0.553 / 0.489 for 1/ 2/ 3/ 4 on the budget-fair poolwhile mean tests passing peaks at 3 (Figure 5, middle panel). Per-run wall-clock stays near the task budget across (Appendix B.6), so total compute grows roughly linearly with , while broadcast traffic rises super-linearly past 3 (Figure 5, right panel). We have not run controlled multi-channel ablation, so whether the decline reflects saturation of the single broadcast channel is an open question rather than an attribution, and the separating ablation is left for future work. The =2 cell is the operational sweet spot under our setup; 3 and 4 pay linearly more compute for declining mean quality. Does mixing models help? Heterogeneous pairing on T4 (Sonnet primary partner) shows 2 Sonnet+Codex at 0.721 (n=3), the highest cell across the heterogeneous combinations we tested, while 2 Sonnet+Gemini reaches only 0.542 (n=3); the pattern suggests heterogeneity is not free lunch: stronger second agent contributes more than weaker one even when the first agent is held fixed, and the coordination layer does not erase capability differences between models  (Table 4)  . 4.6 MCP Chat vs CRDT State What separates the backends? Comparing room backends on T5, the MCP-chat baseline (n=2) fails 1 of 2 runs; score 0.088, zero tests passing, when two agents broadcast file claims simultaneously as free text and neither detects the conflict; the CRDT-state AgentRoom (n=7) succeeds on 7 of 7 because room_claim() returns system-level conflict error. Scope. Sample is small but the qualitative finding (one observed catastrophic chat failure, zero CRDT-state failures) motivates future expansion.

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Coordination, not concurrency, drives the AgentRoom gain. The full six-condition ordering on T4 Sonnet  (Table 1)  and the parallel-merge vs AgentRoom contrast (+0.213, Welch t=3.35, p=0.003) are what 4.2 reports. The bundle is co-designed, and probe separates its components only partially: keeping the CRDT substrate and collaboration prompt but removing the MCP tool surface (Appendix B.13, n=7) lands at 0.588, +0.013 above shared-only. The MCP-tool step accounts for the remaining +0.081 up to AgentRooms 0.669. At these cell sizes the interval on that step spans zero, so we claim the observed mean ordering shared-only < prompt-only < AgentRoom rather than percentage split. The ordering still argues against reading AgentRoom as CRDT plus prompts integration: the largest observed step is the explicit coordination channel; the substrate is the merge primitive on which it stands. AgentRooms claim protocol creates an advisory distributed lock by prompt-level cooperation; the advisory-plus-apology pattern matters because strict locking would block the cross-agent bug-fix case (a teammate correcting an Express 5 routing error in another 8 agents file, Appendix C). The design lineage is advisory locking in distributed systems [Burrows, 2006, Hunt et al., 2010, Gray and Cheriton, 1989]; AgentRooms file-level claim is Chubby-style advisory lock surfaced as an MCP tool, with the agent rather than kernel call as the cooperator. Why not consensus protocol [Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014]? CRDT convergence already provides the safety property advisory claims need; causality is established by the underlying CRDT [Shapiro et al., 2011] which inherits Lamports happens-before [Lamport, 1978] for ordering concurrent edits, in contrast to the operational-transformation lineage [Ellis and Gibbs, 1989, Sun et al., 1998] that requires central transformation server. Cost-equivalent comparison is suggestive. 2Haiku AgentRoom reaches T4 mean 0.662 (n=17) versus 1Sonnet 0.544 (n=32) at roughly half the dollar costWelch t=2.10, p=0.036. This is an actionable hint that paired smaller models can be Pareto-competitive in this difficulty band: the full cross-model headroom matrix (5/6 cells point-estimate-positive, only Haiku T4 clears its bootstrap CI) is what Appendix reports. Activation of collaborative language. AgentRoom logs contain unprompted patternsapologies for boundary violations, proactive gap-filling, do not warnings, dependency documentation (Appendix B, Appendix C). We replay the archived room logs pool-wide to quantify claim-discipline adherence against quality (Appendix B.10). Agents claim modules in 6 of 6 runsthey fix each others bugs in only 2 of 6, and we do not treat that as the typical case. The same prompts produce none of these in the shared-only condition, indicating the channel affordance is necessary; we describe the patterns and do not attempt to attribute them to specific training-data source. Structured state vs unstructured chat. Comparing room backends on T5, MCP-chat (n=2) fails 1/2 runs (score 0.088) when two agents broadcast file claims as free text and neither parses the conflict; CRDT-state AgentRoom (n=7) succeeds 7/7 because room_claim() returns system-level conflict error. The state-management level enforces ownership deterministically where text-parsed claims do not. Paradigm contrast: AgentRoom vs ChatDev-style sequential. The full numbers and Welch test on the same-model same-CLI ChatDev-style three-phase pipeline at matched compute are what 4.3 reports. The contrast isolates the paradigm choice between sequential phase-handoff and concurrent CRDT-coordinated workspace at the same model, CLI, task, and compute, and sequential pipelines amplify the lone-agent failure mode at every phase boundary. complementary prompt-vs-channel control on Haiku (Appendix B) is less conclusive because the structured tool prompt also acts as workflow scaffolding for Haiku and is not separately identified from channel use at this n. Cross-language and cross-domain replication. Does it travel? Two out-of-distribution checks reproduce the direction beyond Express.js/TypeScript: on Rust+axum transposition of T4 (Codex GPT-5.4) AgentRoom 2 matches Solo on the LLM-judge composite (0.740 vs 0.714, n=4 vs 5, descriptive; Appendix B.17), and on 10 DevBench Python multi-file projects (Haiku 4.5) 2 passes 8/10 against Solos 7/10 with zero CRDT semantic conflicts (Appendix B.16). Each is individually underpoweredjointly the direction is not TypeScript-specific. Comparison with prior multi-agent coding systems. CodeCRDT [Pugachev, 2025] and AgentRoom share the CRDT-merged substrate, so what separates them? The two systems propose different coordination paradigms. CodeCRDT is implicit and observation-driven: agents infer teammate state by reading the merged workspace, roles are pre-assigned (outliner / implementer); the empirical question is speedup over sequential baselines (reported bimodal at 21% speedup / 39% slowdown, semantic conflict rate 510%). AgentRoom is explicit: agents negotiate ownership and intent through the room (file-level claim, broadcast log, per-agent status) via MCP tools rather than by re-reading file deltas; the empirical question is failure-mode suppression rather than speedup. The two designs produce different signatures: CodeCRDTs character-level concurrent edits produce the 510% semantic conflicts and the bimodal speed distribution, where AgentRooms file-level claim eliminates concurrent same-file edits (0% semantic conflicts in the headline pool) and the parallel-merge vs AgentRoom matched-compute contrast attributes the gain to the explicit signalling channel rather than to the CRDT substrate. Concurrent industry deployments such as Cursors multi-agent editor, Anthropic Claude Code agent teams, and JetBrains AI Assistant Multi-Agent run the file-claim pattern in production. We claim as the delta here the first matched-compute quantification isolating the coordination layer from parallelism and from the CRDT substrate, on failure mode that neither CodeCRDT nor the shipping systems measure. CodeCRDT and AgentRoom are complementary: CodeCRDTs character-level merge could power AgentRooms intra-file editing within claimed file. 9 Other recent multi-agent coding systems [Pan et al., 2026, Islam et al., 2025, Peng et al., 2026] share the LLM-team-coding goal but use sequential or staged-role paradigms.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Concurrent multi-agent coding has been treated as problem of parallelism or of merge-correct substrate; our position is that it is primarily about explicit coordination. In our matched-compute setting, neither agent count nor the CRDT itself is the main contributor we identify; the difference comes from the runtime rooms state-management operationsfile-level claim, broadcast log, and per-agent status. What can the substrate not do? Without coordination, naive concurrency underperforms single agent; with the substrate alone, agents converge on bytes but not on intent. Within our setting, the substratecoordination separation suggests that an explicit room-style primitive is the contributor we identify, and that matched-compute ablation is how we measure such contributions. Whether the result generalizes beyond coding tasks remains open.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: How far do the statistics reach? The headline results span four backend domains and the three powered CLI-stable models from two providers; per-cell ranges 735, Gemini 3 is underpowered at 5+5, and we exclude Codex-mini (4.4). Pooling the 12 strata under CMH powers the Tier abandonment claim rather than any single cell. Does it hold beyond one runtime? All headline cells share one Express.js/TypeScript runtime; the Rust and Python checks (Appendices B.17, B.16) are bounded mechanism-portability spot checks, not claim of runtime-general magnitude. The parallel-merge vs AgentRoom contrast holds the same Sonnet producer on both sides [Li et al., 2026, Wataoka et al., 2025], and we cross-validate the LLM-judge composite against independent regex and TypeScript-AST scorers (2.5). The cost-equivalent cross-model comparison (Appendix B.6) carries an exposed bias, and we frame it as suggestive. The bundle-component probe reuses the ablation cells (Appendix B.13); we read its substrate-vs-coordination split as indicative, not precise variance decomposition. Quality is assessed by the LLM-judge composite, not an execution oracle: tasks do not ship held-out correctness suite (vitest suites are agent-authored), so we cross-validate the judge against the regex and AST scorers (2.5) but do not claim execution-verified correctness. We replay post-hoc capability probe over the archived T4 snapshots, and it corroborates the ordering endpoints (Appendix B.18). Oracle-free evaluation of in-the-wild software is outside scope. Replication has hosted-model ceiling: we pin CLI versions, model identifiers, and per-agent invocations (3), but hosted models can change server-side, so bit-for-bit reproduction is not claimed; contrasts are matched-CLI and matched-budget, so drift moves both arms together.

sections.content: A.1 Edit-Set Algebra and SEC What is an edit? Let Wt : Σ be the workspace state at time t; each agent keeps local replica kept consistent with peers by the substrate. An edit on file is tuple = (OP, pos, c) with OP {INS, DEL} and payload Σ; the full edit alphabet is E. Token-level edits Etok are those whose payload is the concatenation of one or more BPE/SentencePiece tokens, which is the natural patch granularity an LLM emits. Because every token is contiguous string of characters, Etok embeds losslessly into the character-level Yrs alphabet [Jahns, 2024, Shapiro et al., 2011], so the substrate accepts LLM-generated patches without re-encoding. Sequence or set? standard LLM coding agent produces patch sequence Pseq = (P1, . . . , PT ) with Pt tok sampled from π( Wt1) conditioned on the prior workspace and applied in strict causal order. concurrent multi-agent system instead produces an edit set Econ = {P }i,t with πi( ) sampled in parallel from each agents local replica, then folded into single state WT = MERGE(Econ). Because merge is commutative and associative under the op-based sequence CRDT with Lamport timestamps, the workspace satisfies strong eventual consistency: for any two replicas i, with the same observed operation set O, APPLY(O, 0) = APPLY(O, 0 ). A.2 Information Density How much does one patch carry? Treat each patch as random variable over the rubric coverage {0, 1}D, one bit per scoring dimension; I(P ; X) measures how much single patch contributes to the rubric. For sequential patch sequence the chain rule gives I(Pseq; X) = (cid:80) I(Pt; P<t), and competent LLM avoids redundant edits, so the per-step conditional information I(Pt; P<t) shrinks fast as easy rubric bits are knocked out early. In the concurrent setting with coordination, agents sample at step from posteriors anchored on the same Wt but pushed onto disjoint files by claim, so H(P Wt) for = j, and the per-step joint information across agents , Wt) H(P j I(cid:0){P }N i=1; Wt (cid:1) = (cid:88) i=1 H(P Wt) H(cid:0){P }N i=1 Wt, X(cid:1) (2) scales near-linearly in as long as claims keep the joint entropy from collapsing. Without coordinat tion the agents collide on the same files, H(P ) collapses, and the rate of novel rubric-relevant information per wall-clock step is bottlenecked at the single-agent rate I(P ; X), so the room wastes concurrent compute on redundant edits. This is the information-theoretic reading of the six-condition ablation: AgentRoom delivers higher quality not because individual agents are smarterit is because the coordination layer keeps per-step novel information from collapsing under collision. What does the probe realise? The bundle component probe (5, Appendix B.13) realises this substratecoordination decomposition: removing only the MCP coordination tools while keeping the CRDT substrate and the collaboration prompt recovers +0.013 over shared-only, where the full AgentRoom recovers further +0.081 above the prompt-only cell, and both steps carry wide intervals at these (ordering claim in 5). As check on the reported ordering, we replayed every archived T4 budget-fair snapshot against task-blind capability probe fixed before the replay. sections.title: D Task Specifications
sections.content: All tasks start from the same Express.js 5 sandbox (Node 22, vitest 2, TypeScript 5.6, type: module) with minimal package.json, tsconfig.json, and stub src/server.ts. 3 lists the exact pinned versions. Agents are told the test command, the expected file structure (where prescribed), and the requirements; they are not shown reference solutions. D.1 T1: JWT Authentication System Build complete authentication system from scratch: src/models/user.ts (User interface with id, email, passwordHash, createdAt; UserStore class with in-memory Map storage and create, findByEmail, findById methods; SHA-256 password hashing via crypto.createHash); src/auth/jwt.ts (generateToken, verifyToken, 1-hour expiry, base64 encoding, no external JWT library); src/auth/middleware.ts (Express middleware that extracts Bearer token, verifies it, attaches the user to req, returns 401 on missing or invalid tokens); src/routes/auth.ts (POST /auth/register, POST /auth/login, GET /auth/me); src/server.ts (mount auth routes); and tests/auth.test.ts (seven test cases covering registration, duplicate detection, login success and failure, unauthenticated access, authenticated access, and expired-token handling). TypeScript strict mode; ESM with .js import extensions; 300-second wall-clock budget. D.2 T2: Marketplace API Build marketplace API with user accounts (register, login, profile update), product listings (title, description, price, category, stock count, seller user id), an order system (cart, checkout, status: pending, confirmed, shipped, delivered), review system tied to verified orders, and product search with filters (title keyword, category, price range, minimum rating). Endpoints must return 400, 401, 404, 409 as appropriate. TypeScript strict mode; Express; in-memory storage; ESM with .js extensions. No prescribed file structure: agents must decide how to organize modules, which makes this task sensitive to coordination in the multi-agent setting. 300-second wall-clock budget. D.3 T3: Collaborative E-commerce Build an e-commerce backend API with interconnected modules: User (register, login, profiles), Product (CRUD, search, stock management), Order (cart, checkout, stock validation, status tracking), and Review (purchase-verified ratings, average per product). Full validation, error handling, and integration tests. This task is the same shape as T2 but with tighter cross-module invariants (a review requires delivered order; checkout decrements stock atomically), which stresses inter-agent agreement on shared schemas. D.4 T4: Fintech Ledger Build financial ledger system with: double-entry accounting (every transaction creates debit and credit entries that must balance); multi-currency support (USD, EUR, GBP, JPY with historical exchange rates, amounts stored as integer cents); atomic transaction processing with optimistic locking and rollback; an immutable audit trail with SHA-256 hash chain for tamper detection; reconciliation engine (match internal ledger against external statements); fraud detection rules (threshold amounts, rapid-fire transactions, new counterparties); comprehensive REST API; and tests covering all invariants. 600-second wall-clock budget.

sections.title: E Quality Scorer Details
sections.content: LLM-judge (primary scorer for T4 budget-fair). Who scores run? All continuous-score statistics in the main text on the T4 budget-fair pool are produced by an LLM-judge: single Sonnet 4.6 invocation per run with fixed rubric. The judge receives the task spec, the test command, the test pass/fail status, and the post-run repository snapshot (truncated to 4 KB per file and 30 KB total) and returns four 0100 scores assessing (a) spec coverage (how many spec requirements have visible implementation), (b) correctness signals (proper types, error handling, no obvious bugs), (c) code quality (separation of concerns, naming, idiomatic patterns), and (d) test rigor (edge-case coverage, meaningful assertions). The composite is fixed-weight average (0.35 spec coverage, 0.30 correctness, 0.20 code quality, 0.15 test rigor); weights were fixed before any conditions were evaluated. We scored the full 282 T4 budget-fair pool idempotently, with 14 transient claude -p CLI errors retried until convergence (final 282/282). The rubric and the judge code ship with the released repository. Cross-validation against regex scorer. Why two scorers? We initially used regex-based intrinsic scorer (described below) and rescored every run with the LLM-judge as robustness check. Pearson correlation over the 246 T4 runs that carry both scores is r=0.67 (Figure 10; the LLM-judge pool is 282 runs and the 30700 analysis pool 235-run subset of it; the regex scorer covers subsample of each); the LLM-judge spreads substrate-only conditions slightly more than the regex scorer and tightens the AgentRoom condition. All main directional findings (CMH OR=13.7, AgentRoom > parallel-merge with p<0.01, AgentRoom > ChatDev with p<0.01, 2Haiku Room > 1Sonnet Solo) hold under both scorers. The regex scorer is retained below as secondary scorer and is the primary scorer for the T5 matrix and difficulty gradient; the cross-model effect-size table uses the AST scorer  (Table 2)  . Same-family judge concern. Does the judge favour its own family? The LLM-judge here is Sonnet 4.6, evaluating outputs from mix of distinct models including Haiku 4.5, Codex GPT-5.4, and Gemini 3 Flash, in addition to Sonnet itself. Same-family preference [Li et al., 2026] can inflate Sonnet-vs-other comparisons; the regex/AST cross-validation at r=0.67 provides partial guard, and the parallel-merge vs AgentRoom contrast (both Sonnet) is invariant to that bias because the judge sees the same producer model in both conditions. fully independent third-party judge is left for future work. Regex scorer (secondary, historical). The main paper (2.5) gives the regex scorer composite; this paragraph documents the regex patterns and rationale behind each dimension and weight. Weights 24 Figure 10: The two scorers measure the same thing loosely, not interchangeably. Each point is one T4 run carrying both regex composite and an LLM-judge composite (n=246, the runs scored by both); Pearson r=0.67. The spread off the diagonal is why the body uses one scorer throughout and reports the other as cross-check rather than averaging them. were fixed before any multi-agent runs were evaluated, based on the relative importance of each dimension for production-grade TypeScript code as judged by the authors and not tuned to favour any condition. Type Safety (weight 0.25): counts typed function parameters over total parameters; penalises any annotations (each occurrence subtracts fixed fraction up to the dimension ceiling); rewards interface and type-alias definitions. Rationale: TypeScripts value over JavaScript is precisely the type surface; halving this weight would reward untyped escape hatches. Defensive Coding (weight 0.25): checks for input validation (safeParse, status(400)), 404 handling, error classes, try/catch blocks, null checks, and HTTP status-code diversity. Rationale: production code fails on edge cases; agents that skip validation score artificially high on happy-path tests alone. Test Quality (weight 0.20): counts test cases, assertions per test, error-path tests, and edge-case coverage via keyword search for missing, invalid, duplicate, unauthorized. Rationale: test count alone overrewards trivial tests; assertion density and error-path presence correct this. Design (weight 0.15): file separation ( 3 files), const over let preference, immutable patterns, meaningful comments, middleware usage. Rationale: design choices affect downstream maintainability but are weighted lower because they are partially captured by Type Safety and Defensive Coding already. Test Pass Rate (weight 0.15): fraction of tests passing, parsed from vitests passed failed summary line. Rationale: included at moderate weight so that fully non-compiling output scores near zero without letting trivially small test suite dominate. AST cross-check. Does parser agree with the patterns? As robustness check on our regexbased scorer, we implemented an independent AST-based scorer using the TypeScript compiler API (script released with the paper at scripts/ast_scorer.mjs). The AST scorer counts languagelevel constructs (typed parameters, type alias and interface declarations, try/catch statements, throw statements, validation calls, test calls, function and class declarations) and combines them into composite analogous to our regex scorer. On random sample of 30 runs spanning all tasks, models, 25 and conditions, Pearson correlation between the two scorers is r=0.79 and Spearman rank correlation is ρ=0.62 (n=30). The agreement is far from perfect (in particular the AST scorer treats Codexs compact single-file implementations more harshly than our regex scorer), but the strong correlation supports the use of the regex scorer for the cross-model ES comparisons; runs that the regex scorer rates highly are also rated highly by the AST scorer in the rank-order sense. We do not retire the regex scorer in favor of the AST scorer because the regex scorer is more portable across runtime variants (ESM/CJS, partial syntax, half-finished files), but the cross-check addresses the concern that regex-only scoring could mistakenly reward lexical defensive-coding patterns disconnected from runtime behavior. Leave-one-out sensitivity (alternative solo subset). Table 13 reports robustness check on smaller solo subset (n=4, mean 0.786) than the canonical T4 Sonnet solo used in main Table 1 and Appendix B. We use the smaller subset here because it is the intersection of solo runs for which per-dimension intermediate scorer outputs were retained. The robustness conclusion does not depend on the subset choice: the condition ordering (AgentRoom > solo) is preserved under every single-dimension ablation, with ES ranging from 1.12 to 1.25 on this subset. Table 13: Scorer sensitivity: leave-one-out on T4 (Sonnet 4.6, solo vs 2 AgentRoom). The solo mean reported here (0.786) is computed over smaller subset (4 runs) than the canonical solo subset used in Table 1; the smaller subset is the intersection of solo runs for which we retained per-dimension intermediate scorer outputs at the time of writing, kept here only as robustness check. The AgentRoom > solo ordering is preserved under every single-dimension ablation and the ratio stays within 1.121.25 on this subset. Removed dimension Solo mean 2 mean ES (none, full scorer) Type Safety Defensive Coding Test Quality Design Test Pass Rate 0.786 0.721 0.815 0.854 0.793 0.749 0.928 0.904 0.944 0.956 0.921 0.916 1.18 1.25 1.16 1.12 1.16 1. The composite score follows 2.5; we do not restate the formula here to keep single source of truth. Regex-based scoring was chosen over AST parsing for reproducibility across runtime variants (ESM, CJS, mixed) and because agents occasionally emit near-valid code that an AST parser would reject outright; the trade-off is that the scorer is lexical and can be fooled by appearance of defensive code that is never exercised. We treat this as known limitation in the Discussion and as direction for future work.
